findings.description: The change calls `env.canReferenceType(ref)` on `ReferenceEmitEnvironment`, but the diff does not add that method or touch the environment class. If it is not already defined, this will not compile. The replacement `canReferenceType` check must also match the old `checkIfClassIsExported` semantics for exported classes, including ones exported via `export {}` and via aliases. Otherwise some non-exported classes may be treated as referenceable and get a non-inline TCB, or the reverse.

The new skip condition is too broad. `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true when any placeholder appears anywhere in the part, and `selector[res.index + 1]` is tested against hex characters for every separator type. SafeSelector also uses placeholders for attribute selectors such as `[attr]`, for `:nth-*` expressions, and for escaped selectors. So `input[type=text] a {}`, `.foo[bar] div {}`, `[x]>b` and `.one\:two div` are all wrongly treated as 'not a separator' when the next token starts with a-f or a digit. The descendant or child combinator is then swallowed and the following compound selector is never scoped. This regresses ordinary selectors, because those parts would no longer get the `[contenta]` attribute. The check should apply only when the separator is a space and the part ends with an escape placeholder.

The guard `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true for any placeholder, not only one created for an escaped hex sequence. SafeSelector also replaces attribute selectors such as `[type=text]` and `:nth-*(...)` arguments with `__ph-N__`. A descendant combinator after one of those, followed by an element name that starts with a hex character, is therefore wrongly treated as an escape-terminating space. Examples are `[x] div`, `a[href] em` and `input[type=text] button`. The separator is skipped and the parts are not scoped separately, so the second compound selector loses its `[contenta]` attribute. This regresses component style encapsulation for common selectors. The check should confirm that the placeholder is an escape (backslash plus hex digits) at the end of `part`.

The new skip condition is far too broad. It fires whenever the pending `part` contains any `__ph-N__` placeholder and the character after the separator is a hex digit. It does not check that the placeholder is an escape sequence, that the separator is a space, or that the placeholder ends the part. Placeholders are also used for attribute selectors (`[attr]`) and `:nth-*(...)` expressions. So `[type=text] button {}`, `div[foo] a {}`, `.x:nth-child(2n+1) b {}` and `.a\:b .c {}` are all treated as one compound selector. The descendant combinator is swallowed and the preceding part is never scoped. This is a regression: `[type=text] button` now becomes `[type=text] button[contenta]` instead of `[type=text][contenta] button[contenta]`, breaking style encapsulation. The check also ignores the separator type, so `.a\:b>a`, `.a\:b+b` and `.a\:b~c` (with `>`, `+`, `~` as the separator) are skipped as well.

The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework defines these globals (for example when it ends up in a server bundle, or in a non-Jasmine/Mocha runner), module evaluation throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code tolerated this case.

The old code guarded with `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)`. The new code calls `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework globals exist, for example when the file ends up in a server bundle or a non-Jasmine/Mocha/Jest runner, evaluating the module throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. This is a regression from the previously safe behavior.

The old `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework has defined these globals (e.g. server bundles, a non-Jasmine/Mocha runner, or a tool that loads the module), it throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code tolerated this case. This is a behavior regression, not a pure refactor.

In `collectDeferredSymbols`, `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never updated. It is initialised to `false` in the dependency collection and the loop only sets `isDeferrable` and `importPath`. The `isDefaultImport` value goes only into the `deferrableTypes` map. The compiler paths that read `deferredDep.isDefaultImport` or `dep.isDefaultImport` (`template.ts`, `create_defer_deps_fns.ts`) therefore always emit `m => m.CmpA`. For a default-imported component that resolves to `undefined` at runtime, which breaks the lazy-loaded dependency function. The new test expecting `m => m.default` in `TestCmp_Defer_1_DepsFn` would fail. The fix is to set `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)`.

`isDefaultImport` treats an import as default only when there are no named bindings. For `import Default, {Other} from './x'`, `namedBindings` is defined, so it returns false. A deferred default-imported symbol then gets `m.Symbol` instead of `m.default`. The check is per declaration, not per identifier.

isDefaultImport() returns true only when the import has no namedBindings. For a mixed import such as `import CmpA, {Other} from './cmp-a'`, or `import {default as CmpA} from './cmp-a'`, namedBindings is defined, so a default-bound symbol is reported as non-default. The generated dynamic import then uses `m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. Conversely, with `import Default, {Named}`, the check does not look at which binding the symbol actually uses.

isDefaultImport() returns false whenever the import has named bindings. For a combined import such as `import CmpA, {Other} from './cmp-a'`, where CmpA is the default import and is used in a @defer block or deferredImports, the generated loader becomes `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`. At runtime that resolves to undefined and the deferred dependency fails to load.

The post-schedule restore of `once` now uses `taskData.options.once = true`. `taskData` is a shared global object, so `taskData.options` can be overwritten if `scheduleEventTask` or a zone hook (such as `onScheduleTask`) triggers a nested `addEventListener`. In that case the `once` flag would be set on the wrong options object, or the local `options` would never get `once` restored. The previous code used the local `options` reference, which is safe against this.

The condition is inverted. `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary() } else { setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0') }` now sets tabindex=0 on real anchor and area elements and skips it for non-anchor hosts such as div or button. Non-anchor routerLink elements lose keyboard focusability, which is an accessibility regression. The subscribe call is also a no-op there, because it returns early for non-anchors.

The subscription condition for the case with no `queryParamsHandling` on the link is inverted. It subscribes when the router's default handling is NOT merge/preserve, and skips the subscription when the default IS 'merge' or 'preserve'. With `defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge'` or `'preserve'` and no per-link setting, the href depends on current router state but never updates on NavigationEnd. The href goes stale after query params change.

The condition in the constructor is inverted. `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { this.subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary(); } else { this.setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0'); }`. For non-anchor hosts the helper returns immediately, so the call does nothing. For anchor hosts (`<a>`, `<area>`, compatible custom elements) the else branch runs and sets `tabindex="0"` on a natively focusable element, which is a behavior regression. Anchors also skip the NavigationEnd subscription in the constructor, so href is only subscribed after the first ngOnChanges. Non-anchor elements still get the tabindex. The condition should be `if (this.isAnchorElement)`.

The condition for subscribing to NavigationEnd is inverted. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes when the default does NOT depend on router state, and skips it when the router-wide `defaultQueryParamsHandling` is 'merge' or 'preserve'. In that case a link with no per-link handling has an href that depends on the current query params, but it never updates after navigation, so the href goes stale. It also creates needless subscriptions for plain links. It should be `!this.queryParamsHandling && dependsOnRouterState(default)`.

The constructor branches are swapped. `if (!this.isAnchorElement) subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary() else setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` calls the subscribe helper only for non-anchors, where it returns immediately. It calls the tabindex setter only for anchors, where it also returns immediately. The original constructor-time `tabindex=0` for non-anchor hosts is lost, and no subscription is created in the constructor for anchors. Anchors now depend entirely on ngOnChanges for the subscription.

The `firstValueFrom` replacement uses `first()`, which errors with EmptyError when the source completes without emitting. The `toPromise()` it replaces resolved with `undefined` in that case. A `redirectTo` function returning an empty observable (for example `EMPTY`) used to resolve to `undefined`. It now rejects the promise with EmptyError, and the navigation fails with an error instead of going through the previous handling. The same applies to the other call sites in `recognize.ts` if a source completes empty.

The "different DOM parent" condition cancels and force-removes leaving elements that have nothing to do with the new element. leavingNodes is keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance of a component or template. If instance A's element is still animating out in parent X and instance B is created in parent Y, B's insert finds A with a different parent. A's leave animation is then cancelled and the element removed. This breaks legitimate leave animations for reused components, for example the same component rendered in two places.

The previousSibling check is only a heuristic for an @if toggle. When a leaving element is adjacent to a newly inserted element of the same TNode, it is cancelled even though it is a different logical item. An example is an @for list where one item leaves and a new item is inserted immediately after it, or a whole list is replaced. The leaving element's animation is cut short and the element removed early.

The removal of removeAnimationsFromQueue means enter animations still queued for a node are no longer dequeued when that node is removed. If the node is removed before the animation queue flushes, for example on a quick toggle, the stale enter animation functions still run against a detached or leaving element. This can add enter classes or listeners to a node that is leaving, and can interfere with the leave animation.

cancelLeavingNodes is called on every native insert of every node, including text and comment nodes and nodes in apps that use no animations. The rNode is cast to HTMLElement, and the function and the leavingNodes map are now pulled into every bundle (the golden symbols changed in all of them). Because the same function runs for every insert, this adds overhead and a coupling to the animation code on a hot path.

`leavingNodes` is keyed by `tNode`, which is shared by every instance of a template or component, and `cancelLeavingNodes` now treats any leaving element with a different DOM parent as a duplicate. If instance A is leaving in parent P1 and another instance of the same template is inserted into P2, A's leave animation is cut short. This happens for lists of components or embedded views that each have `animate.leave` and sit in different hosts. `animationend` is dispatched with `cancel: true` and A is removed immediately, which is a regression for unrelated instances. The overlay heuristic is too broad for this.

The code that removed queued enter animations from the animation queue when a node is detached has been deleted, as has `removeAnimationsFromQueue`. If an element is created and then removed before the queue is flushed, its enter animation functions still run against a detached element. This can cause errors or stale animation state on removed nodes. Nothing else cancels those queued functions.

trackLeavingNodes is called on every Detach of a node whose TNode has a leave animation. That includes plain detaches and moves such as @for reordering or ViewContainerRef.move, where the element is reinserted and no leave animation ever runs. The live element then stays in `leavingNodes` and is never cleared. A later Insert for the same TNode, such as a newly added @for item placed right after it, sees that element as `previousSibling`. `cancelLeavingNodes` then dispatches a cancel event and calls `removeChild` on a live, visible element. The stale entries also keep detached elements alive.

The 'different DOM parent' heuristic is wrong because `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance of a component or template. When one instance's element is animating out in parent X and another instance of the same component inserts its element in a different parent Y, the new insert cancels and force-removes the first instance's leaving element. This cuts off a legitimate leave animation, for example in lists of components that each use @if with animate.leave. The check cannot tell the overlay/portal case from unrelated instances.

The removal of `removeAnimationsFromQueue` means a queued enter animation is no longer dropped when the element is detached before the queue flushes. With rapid toggling, the enter animation can still run on an element that is already leaving. It adds enter classes to it, may register enter listeners, and `cleanupEnterClassData` may interfere with the leave animation. This is a behavioral regression for quick toggles in the same parent.

The serialization format of `position` changed. Previously the array was interpolated into a quoted string, which produced a comma-separated value like '0,1,2'. Now `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]". The diff does not change `findConstructorByPosition` or `findDomElementByPosition`. If those still parse with `split(',').map(Number)`, the first and last elements become NaN, and 'view source' and 'select DOM element' break. The same format change applies to `selectDomElement` at line 26.

`position` is an array, and the old template literal turned it into a comma-separated string like `0,1,2`. The receiving `findConstructorByPosition` most likely parses that with `split(',')`. `stringifyAndEscape(position)` now sends the JSON text `"[0,1,2]"`, so the split yields `[0`, `1` and `2]`, and `parseInt` returns NaN for the first and last. View Source then resolves the wrong element or fails. The change touches only this file, so the receiver was not updated to match.

`selectDomElement` has the same problem. The position is now passed as a JSON-array string (`"[0,1]"`) instead of the comma-joined string (`0,1`). If `findDomElementByPosition` still parses it with `split(',')` and `parseInt`, the indices become NaN and selecting the DOM element breaks.

`position` is an ElementPosition (number[]). It used to be interpolated as `'${position}'`, which produces a comma-joined string like "0,1,2". The receiving `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` helpers most likely parse that format with `split(',').map(parseInt)`. `stringifyAndEscape(position)` now passes the string "[0,1,2]" instead. Splitting it on commas gives "[0" and "2]", and parseInt turns "[0" into NaN, so the lookup fails. 'View source' and 'select DOM element' would then break. Only the sender was changed, and the receivers were not updated to JSON.parse. The fix is to serialize with `JSON.stringify(position.join(','))`, or update the receivers.

`selectDomElement` has the same problem. The position array is now sent as a JSON-array string ("[0,1]") where the receiver expects a comma-separated list of indexes ("0,1"). The first index is parsed as NaN, so the element cannot be found.

The spec imports setParseTemplateAsSourceFileForTest and resetParseTemplateAsSourceFileForTest from '../diagnostics'. The diff never touches the typecheck/diagnostics index.ts to re-export them from './src/diagnostic'. If the index only lists named exports, the import fails to compile or is undefined, which breaks the spec and its afterEach hook.

If the native set function returns a non-number falsy value (undefined or null), the new code reads `handleOrId.refresh` and throws a TypeError. The old code explicitly tolerated this, with a comment about polyfills and browsers returning undefined from setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate or requestAnimationFrame, and it then returned the task. `scheduleTask` now crashes for those environments, which is a regression. The fix is to guard with `handleOrId && isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)`.

`scheduleTask` now assumes any non-number result from the native setter is an object. If a polyfill or environment returns `undefined` or `null` (the old code explicitly allowed this), `handleOrId.refresh` throws a TypeError while scheduling. Previously such timers worked and `task` was returned instead. This is a regression for those environments.

`scheduleTask` now calls `handleOrId.refresh` for any non-number return value. Some polyfills and browsers return `undefined` or `null` from `setTimeout`, `setInterval` or `setImmediate`, and the old code explicitly tolerated that. With such a value, `isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)` throws a TypeError during scheduling. The task then moves to the unknown state and the error is rethrown to the caller. This is a regression for environments with non-standard timer implementations.

The patched `refresh` re-increments the task count whenever the task is `notScheduled`. After `clearTimeout`, `cancelTask` has already set `task._zoneDelegates = null` via `_updateTaskCount(-1)`. Calling `timeout.refresh()` on a cleared Timeout (Node allows this) then calls `zone._updateTaskCount(task, 1)` and dereferences a null `zoneDelegates`, which throws a TypeError. Only the `runTask` path restores `_zoneDelegates`. Also, the task is marked `scheduled` again but `id[taskSymbol]` was nulled, so the refreshed timer can no longer be cleared through zone.js.

The `runCount++` was removed from `runTask` and moved into `ZoneTask.invokeTask`. Microtasks are executed by `drainMicroTaskQueue` calling `zone.runTask` directly, so their `runCount` is now never incremented. The count also changes meaning: it is no longer reset to 0 after a non-periodic task finishes, and it is incremented even when `runTask` returns early for a `notScheduled` task. Any code or zone spec that relies on `runCount` could observe different behavior.

The global utility is registered only through a bare side-effect import (`import './router_devtools';`). The router package is published with `sideEffects: false`, so bundlers such as webpack and esbuild may drop this import. The `ɵgetLoadedRoutes` global would then never be published, and DevTools would not find it. The registration also runs unconditionally at module load, so it is not guarded by dev mode and cannot be tree-shaken from production builds.

The global function is registered only through a bare side-effect import (`import './router_devtools'`) that runs a top-level `ɵpublishExternalGlobalUtil` call. The router package is published with `sideEffects: false`, so bundlers and the Angular optimizer may drop this import and its top-level call. `ɵgetLoadedRoutes` would then never be published in optimized builds, and DevTools would not find it. In dev builds the call may also be a no-op depending on how core gates it.

`normalizeBootstrapOptions` uses `hostElementOrOptions instanceof Element`, which breaks in two cases. On the server (platform-server/domino, Node), `Element` is not a defined global. If `bootstrap()` is called with anything other than `undefined` or a string, this throws `ReferenceError: Element is not defined`. Elements from another realm (an iframe), or DOM implementations whose elements aren't instances of the global `Element`, fail the check too. They fall through and are treated as an options object, so `hostElement` is `undefined`. The component then bootstraps onto its selector instead of the element passed in, or throws.

A `null` argument is not handled. The old signature accepted `any`, and `document.querySelector(...)` returning null used to fall back to the component selector. Now `null` fails the `undefined`/string/Element checks and is returned as the options object. The caller's destructuring `const {hostElement, directives, bindings} = ...` then throws a TypeError. This is a runtime regression for existing JS callers and for callers who cast. The example change to `element!` shows the type is now stricter.

normalizeBootstrapOptions only handles undefined, string and `Element`. `null` (for example the result of `document.querySelector(...)`, which used to fall back to the component selector) is returned as-is, and the destructuring in bootstrapImpl then throws `TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'hostElement' of null`. Untyped callers, and callers using `any` or casts, previously worked and now crash at runtime instead of falling back.

Detecting a host element with `instanceof Element` is fragile. Elements from another realm (iframe or popup), or non-Element nodes accepted by the renderer, are treated as an options object. Their `hostElement` is then undefined, so bootstrap silently falls back to the selector lookup, or fails to find a host. In environments where a global `Element` is not defined (some SSR or worker setups), the `instanceof` check itself throws a ReferenceError.

`normalizeBootstrapOptions` decides between a host element and an options object with `hostElementOrOptions instanceof Element`. Two cases break. (1) A real DOM element from another realm (an iframe, or a different document/window) fails the `instanceof` check, so it is treated as an options object. `hostElement`, `directives` and `bindings` are then all undefined, and bootstrap silently falls back to the component selector, so the element is ignored. (2) A `null` argument (e.g. an unchecked `document.querySelector(...)` result, which JS users and `any`-typed callers could previously pass) skips every branch and is returned as the options object. The destructuring `{hostElement, directives, bindings} = null` then throws a TypeError instead of falling back to the selector as before. In addition, `Element` is referenced as a global, which can throw a ReferenceError in non-DOM environments such as SSR without DOM globals.

For `legend` tags, `attrs` is no longer copied into a new dict because the `{**attrs, "for": ...}` step is skipped. The `required_css_class` block that follows then does `attrs["class"] += ...` or `attrs["class"] = ...` on the caller's own dict. When `legend_tag(attrs=...)` is called with a required field and a form that sets `required_css_class`, the caller's dict is mutated. Reusing that dict, for example across several fields, makes the `required` class accumulate. Before this change the dict was always copied when `id_for_label` was set.

For tag == "legend", `attrs` is no longer copied. Previously `{**attrs, "for": ...}` always produced a fresh dict. Now `attrs = attrs or {}` leaves the caller's dict in place. If the field is required and the form has `required_css_class`, the following `attrs["class"] += ...` or `attrs["class"] = ...` mutates the caller's dict. Reusing one attrs dict across several `legend_tag(attrs=...)` calls, such as a shared dict in a template tag or loop, makes the class list grow with each call (`foo required required ...`). It also leaks `required_css_class` into fields that are not required. This is a regression from the old copy behavior.

The raw-block regexes are stricter than the old tokenization. `_raw_start_re` needs `\s+` after `{%`, and the `comment` and unnamed `verbatim` end regexes need `[^\S\n]+` between `{%` and `endcomment`/`endverbatim`. The old lexer and parser accepted `{%verbatim%}...{%endverbatim%}` and `{%endcomment%}` because they compared the stripped content. Now `{%verbatim%}` is not detected at all, so its content is tokenized as live template syntax. A comment closed with `{%endcomment%}` is never closed, so the rest of the template is swallowed as text and parsing fails with an unclosed tag. This regresses existing templates that omit the spaces.

The new closing-tag regexes for comment and unnamed verbatim blocks require at least one whitespace character after `{%` (`[^\S\n]+`). `_raw_start_re` likewise requires `\s+` after `{%`. Tags written without spaces, such as `{%endcomment%}` or `{%endverbatim%}`, are still valid block tags and are matched by `tag_re`, and the parser accepts them. Once any raw-aware path is taken, for example because another `{% comment %}` appears in the template, the lexer treats `{%endcomment%}` as plain text instead of the closing tag. The parser then never sees the end token and raises 'Unclosed tag' or swallows the rest of the template. Likewise a `{%verbatim%}` opener is not detected as raw. Templates that rendered correctly before are therefore broken. The named-verbatim regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, which is inconsistent with these.

The closing-tag regexes `_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` require at least one non-newline whitespace character between `{%` and `endcomment`/`endverbatim`. The old lexer compared the stripped tag content, so `{%endverbatim%}` and `{%endcomment%}` worked. The opener is still recognized without whitespace, because `_raw_end_tag_re` strips the content. As a result, `{%verbatim%}...{%endverbatim%}` (or `{%comment%}...{%endcomment%}`) in debug mode, or in any template that also has a spaced opener, never finds its closer. The rest of the template is treated as text and the parser raises an unclosed-tag error. Behaviour also depends on the code path: the fast path in `tokenize()` is chosen only when no whitespace-separated opener exists, and `DebugLexer` always uses the raw-aware splitter. Named verbatim closers use `[^\S\n]*`, so they are inconsistent with unnamed ones.

orderby_issubset_groupby resolves every string in order_by with F(order_by). Strings with a descending prefix ("-id", "-name"), the random ordering "?", and strings with a table-qualified or extra reference are not valid F() names. For a grouped query such as `Book.objects.values('contact__name').annotate(c=Count('id')).order_by('-contact__name').count()`, resolving F('-contact__name') raises FieldError ("Cannot resolve keyword '-contact__name'"). Before this change count() simply cleared the ordering and worked, so this is a crash regression for common order_by usage. The code needs to strip the '-' prefix and handle '?' and similar cases, for example by using the same order-by normalization as the compiler.

Descending order_by strings such as "-id" are passed to F(order_by).resolve_expression(q). F does not parse the "-" prefix, so this raises FieldError (Cannot resolve keyword '-id'). "?" for random ordering fails the same way. Calling .count() or .aggregate() on a values().annotate() queryset with an explicit group_by and .order_by('-field') will therefore crash. Before this change, the ordering was cleared without being resolved. Resolved OrderBy expressions also never compare equal to the Col objects in group_by, so descending ordering is never treated as a subset.

orderby_issubset_groupby wraps each string order_by entry in F(...).resolve_expression(). order_by strings can carry a '-' direction prefix or be '?', for example order_by('-id') or order_by('?'). F('-id') cannot be resolved to a field, so it raises FieldError (Cannot resolve keyword '-id'). This is reached from get_aggregation() for any query with a tuple group_by (values().annotate()) and a descending string ordering, so .count() or .aggregate() on such querysets now crashes. They worked before this change.

alogin() no longer updates request.user. The old `if hasattr(request, "user"): request.user = user` block was replaced by an `auser` override, not extended with one. After `await alogin(request, user)`, synchronous code that reads `request.user` (templates, context processors, sync middleware or views) still sees the old user, usually AnonymousUser. This regresses existing behavior. Both `user` and `auser` should be updated.

alogout() no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser. After `await alogout(request)`, `request.user` still holds the logged-out user, so later code that reads it treats the request as authenticated. This is a regression and a security concern. Only `request.auser` is replaced. Both attributes should be reset.

alogin() no longer sets request.user. The old `if hasattr(request, "user"): request.user = user` block was replaced by one that only updates request.auser. After `await alogin(request, user)`, request.user keeps the old user, usually AnonymousUser. This is a regression for existing async code and for sync code that reads request.user afterwards. It also leaves request.user and request.auser disagreeing. The fix should update both attributes.

alogout() no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser. Only request.auser is replaced. After `await alogout(request)`, request.user still refers to the previously authenticated user. Views, templates and permission checks that read request.user in the rest of the request will still treat the user as logged in. This is a regression and a security-relevant inconsistency with the sync logout().

alogin() used to set request.user, and the patch replaces that with a request.auser override. Nothing updates request.user any more. With AuthenticationMiddleware, request.user stays the old user (or AnonymousUser) after alogin(), so sync code and templates that read request.user see stale data. Any request with only `user` set and no `auser` is not updated at all. Upstream's fix sets both attributes.

alogout() no longer resets request.user to AnonymousUser. It only replaces request.auser. After alogout(), request.user still holds the logged-out user, which is a security-relevant regression: later code or templates in the same request still see an authenticated user. Requests that have `user` but no `auser` are also not reset.

`sort_keys=False` is now hard-coded next to `**self.options`. If a caller passes `sort_keys` through `serializers.serialize('yaml', ..., sort_keys=...)`, `yaml.dump` receives the keyword twice and raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Previously the option was accepted, because the dict representer ignored it. Using `self.options.setdefault('sort_keys', False)` would avoid the crash.

`sort_keys=False` is now passed explicitly alongside `**self.options`. If a caller passes `sort_keys` as a serializer option, e.g. `serializers.serialize('yaml', qs, sort_keys=True)`, `yaml.dump` receives the keyword twice and raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Before this change the option was accepted, because the dict representer ignored it. The fix is to use `self.options.setdefault('sort_keys', False)` instead of a hard-coded keyword.

`sort_keys=False` is hard-coded next to `**self.options`. If a caller passes `sort_keys` through `serializers.serialize('yaml', ..., sort_keys=...)`, `yaml.dump` now raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Before this change the option was accepted and had no effect, so this is a small backwards-compatibility regression. Using `self.options.setdefault('sort_keys', False)` would avoid it.

PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode now runs force_str(password), which decodes bytes as UTF-8. Before this change, pbkdf2() accepted arbitrary bytes passwords through force_bytes. A bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 now raises UnicodeDecodeError, which is a regression for callers that passed raw bytes. The password only needs to be converted to bytes for hashing, so the decode step is unnecessary. The salt does need to be str, because it is embedded in the encoded string.

PBKDF2PasswordHasher.encode() now calls force_str(password) before pbkdf2(). A bytes password that is not valid UTF-8 now raises UnicodeDecodeError, for example make_password(b'\xff\xfe') or check_password(b'\xff', encoded). Before this change, pbkdf2() applied force_bytes() to the password and hashed the raw bytes without trouble. This regresses the default hasher, since it needlessly round-trips bytes through str. The password should stay as bytes, or be converted with force_bytes() only.

`DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` matches a single DNS label only. The new `simple_url_2_re` omits `DomainNameValidator.domain_re`, which covers the additional dotted labels. As a result, bare multi-label domains such as `sub.example.com`, `docs.djangoproject.com/path` and `mail.example.net` no longer match. The old pattern `\w[^@]+\.(com|...)` accepted them, so `urlize` stops linking them. This is a regression for existing users. The pattern should be `hostname_re` followed by `(?:domain_re)` and then the TLD.

`DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` matches only a single DNS label with no dots. `domain_re`, which matches the further `.label` parts, is not included. The new `simple_url_2_re` therefore only matches `label.tld`, such as `example.com`. Bare multi-label hosts like `sub.example.com`, `mail.example.co.com` or `foo.bar.org/path` (no scheme, no `www.`) no longer match, so `urlize` stops linking them. This regresses previously working behavior. The pattern needs `(?:{DomainNameValidator.domain_re})` between the hostname part and the TLD.

`DomainNameValidator.hostname_re` matches a single DNS label with no dots. The new `simple_url_2_re` is `^(?!http)<one label>\.(com|edu|...)($|/.*)$`, so it only accepts `label.tld`. Words with subdomains and no `www.` or scheme, such as `docs.djangoproject.com`, `mail.google.com` or `foo.example.org/path`, used to be urlized and now are left as plain text. `DomainNameValidator.domain_re` (the repeated `.label` part) needs to be included between the hostname and the TLD.

The new wrapper is always a plain synchronous function. When `non_atomic_requests` is applied to an `async def` view, the result is no longer a coroutine function, so `iscoroutinefunction` returns False. Django's handler will then treat the view as sync and run it in a thread, and it will get back an un-awaited coroutine instead of an HttpResponse. Async views decorated with `@non_atomic_requests` therefore break with an error like 'didn't return an HttpResponse object. It returned an unawaited coroutine'. This is a regression for existing users, and the wrapper needs an async variant.

The new wrapper is always a plain synchronous function. When `non_atomic_requests` is applied to an `async def` view, `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction(wrapper)` returns False. Django then treats the view as sync. Under ASGI it is run through `sync_to_async`, and under WSGI it is called directly. Either way the view returns an unawaited coroutine, which gives "didn't return an HttpResponse ... returned an unawaited coroutine" errors. This is a regression for existing async views decorated with `@non_atomic_requests`, which previously worked because the original function was returned. The fix needs an async wrapper for coroutine functions.

The new wrapper is always a plain synchronous `def`. When `non_atomic_requests` is applied to an `async def` view, the result is no longer a coroutine function. It is a sync function that returns an unawaited coroutine. Django's handlers use `iscoroutinefunction(view)` to decide how to adapt the view. Under ASGI the view would be run in a thread and return a coroutine object, which raises 'didn't return an HttpResponse object... unawaited coroutine'. Under WSGI, `async_to_sync` would not be applied. Async views decorated with `@non_atomic_requests` therefore break, which is a regression. The wrapper needs to be an `async def` (or be marked as a coroutine function) when `view` is async.

In the new non-endpoint, no-converter branch, `path.startswith(self._route)` and `path.removeprefix(self._route)` use `self._route` directly. For translated routes (`path(_('translated/'), include(...))`) it is a lazy string proxy, not a `str`. `str.startswith` raises `TypeError` for it, so resolving any include-style prefix with a lazily translated route crashes. The old regex path handled this through `LocaleRegexDescriptor`, which evaluates the translation for the active language. The new code should use `str(self._route)`. Matching also ignores the active language, because `converters` is computed once.

For non-endpoint routes without converters, `path.startswith(self._route)` and `path.removeprefix(self._route)` use `self._route` directly. For translated routes (`gettext_lazy`) this is a lazy proxy, not a `str`, so both calls raise `TypeError`. The old code went through `self.regex`, which resolved the translation via `LocaleRegexDescriptor`. This also ignores the active language, because it never uses the translated value. It would break `include()` or prefix patterns with lazy-translated routes such as `path(_('translated/'), include(...))`. Wrapping the route in `str()` would avoid the crash.

The new converter-less branches use self._route directly, but for translated routes (path(_('translated/'), ...)) it is a lazy proxy, not a str. `path.startswith(self._route)` and `path.removeprefix(self._route)` raise TypeError for a lazy proxy, so non-endpoint patterns such as translated include() prefixes would crash on resolve. The old regex path avoided this by using str(route) and the language-specific regex. The endpoint `==` comparison and the prefix check also don't explicitly evaluate the lazy string for the active language. The fix is to use str(self._route) at match time.

`_route_to_regex` is now wrapped in `lru_cache` and returns a mutable `converters` dict. `RoutePattern` stores that same dict as `self.converters`, so every pattern with an identical route string shares one dict. `URLResolver._populate` mutates it in place with `sub_pattern.pattern.converters.update(current_converters)`. Converters from one namespaced include can therefore leak into the cached entry and into unrelated patterns with the same route. Before this change each call built a fresh dict. The effect is limited to extra keys in `converters`, so the practical impact is likely small.
